cases.label: suppressor-anger
cases.reasoning: An avoidant, cooperative, low-autonomy personality facing moderate anger will almost certainly default to suppressing the expression to avoid confrontation and preserve harmony — this is the quintessential response modulation profile, and moderate intensity keeps it well within their execution capacity.
cases.narrative: You feel the anger coil tight in your chest — the injustice is real, and every nerve wants to snap back. But you hold it. You press your jaw closed, slow your breathing, let the heat pool behind your ribs without letting it reach your voice or your hands. The anger doesn't dissolve — it sits there, fully formed, a clenched fist behind a calm face. You know the unfairness. You choose not to perform the knowing. There's a deliberate stillness you're wearing like armour, and beneath it the indignation pulses steady, waiting for a channel you haven't yet decided to give it.

cases.label: suppressor-shame
cases.reasoning: An avoidant personality would naturally gravitate toward distraction to escape shame's discomfort, but their moderate-rules and self-standards orientation makes cognitive change (reappraisal of the failure's meaning) a more natural and effective fit — avoidance of the emotion through attentional deployment delays resolution of the standards-gap that caused the shame in the first place.
cases.temporalReasoning: Pure temporal containment — the narrative depicts riding out shame through attentional withdrawal and waiting for intensity to fade ('when the sting has faded enough'), with no cognitive restructuring, belief challenging, or reappraisal of the standards that triggered the shame.
cases.narrative: You feel the shame land — that quiet, inward collapse when you see the gap between what you expected of yourself and what you delivered. Your gaze drops. Your thoughts start to curl inward, replaying the failure, measuring you against your own yardstick. But something older than deliberation takes over: you pull away. Not from the room, but from the thought. Your attention slides sideways, finding the texture of what's around you — the task still waiting, the next small thing that doesn't require you to look at yourself. The withdrawal isn't a decision so much as a reflex, a door closing softly before the draught gets in. The self-evaluation is still there, folded and set aside like a letter you'll read later, when the sting has faded enough to hold it steady. For now, you simply step back from the mirror.

cases.label: reappraiser-anger
cases.reasoning: An analytical, high-autonomy personality with strict rule-following has exactly the cognitive toolkit to reappraise a controllable injustice — they'll systematically reframe the situation through principled reasoning, and moderate intensity keeps the emotion well within the range where reappraisal is executable and effective.
cases.narrative: You feel the anger sharpen — the injustice clear, the unfairness obvious, the impulse to push back already forming in your throat. But before the words arrive, a quieter thought cuts across: you've seen this shape before. The situation is controllable, which means the story you're telling yourself — that this was done to you, that you're cornered — isn't the only reading. You turn the frame. Maybe the slight wasn't aimed. Maybe the constraint has a logic you haven't asked about yet. The reappraisal doesn't erase the anger so much as loosen its grip on the narrative — the facts haven't changed, but the meaning you've draped over them shifts, and with it the urgency drains. The injustice might still be real, but it's smaller now, one interpretation among several rather than the only possible truth. You feel the heat step back from your skin, settling into something cooler and more deliberate — not agreement, but the recognition that you have room to choose what this means before you choose what to do about it.

cases.label: reappraiser-reproach
cases.reasoning: An analytical, high-autonomy personality can effectively reappraise reproach by reasoning about why the other person fell short, but their strict rule-following nature means they genuinely believe the standard was violated — situation modification (addressing the failure directly through cooperative correction) would be slightly more natural for someone who both enforces rules and has the autonomy to act on them.
cases.narrative: You feel the reproach settle in — that crisp, judgmental clarity where someone else's failure sits measured against your own standards and comes up short. The assessment feels clean, almost righteous: they should have known better, should have done better, and the fact that they didn't is a mark against them. But then the reappraisal begins, not as a defence of the other person but as a quiet interrogation of the frame you've placed around them. Your standards are yours — earned, tested, real — but they were built on ground this person may never have stood on. The failure you're seeing might look different from behind their eyes: a constraint you can't see, a priority you haven't weighed, a capacity you're assuming they share with you. The reproach doesn't vanish — it thins. The sharp edge of judgment softens into something more provisional, more like a question than a verdict. You still see the gap between what was done and what you'd have done, but the meaning of that gap has shifted from indictment to information. They fell short of your measure. That's a fact about the distance between you, not necessarily a fact about their character.

cases.label: anyone-fear
cases.reasoning: An avoidant, low-autonomy personality facing an uncontrollable threat has neither the assertiveness to modify the situation nor the sense of agency to reappraise it as manageable — redirecting attention away from the threat is both their natural default and the empirically supported strategy for uncontrollable stressors at moderate intensity.
cases.narrative: You feel the fear take hold — that cold tightening behind the sternum, the way the threat fills your peripheral vision until it's all you can see. The uncontrollable part is the worst of it: your mind keeps running scenarios and every one of them ends the same way, with you unable to change the outcome. The loop is consuming you. So you redirect. Not toward a solution — there isn't one to reach for — but away from the grinding rehearsal of helplessness. You pull your attention like a searchlight turning from a dark horizon toward something closer, smaller, solid. What's in front of you right now. The texture of the present moment, where the threat hasn't arrived yet and your hands still have something to do. The fear doesn't leave — it remains at the edge, a low hum in the architecture of your awareness — but you've stopped feeding it the full beam of your focus. The threat is still real, still beyond your control, but your mind is no longer pinned to it. You've given yourself a narrow corridor of attention where the uncontrollable thing is not the only thing, and in that corridor you can breathe again, think again, be something other than afraid.

cases.label: incoherent-anger
cases.reasoning: The flexible-rules and independent traits provide genuine cognitive reappraisal capacity — they can reframe the contradiction as legitimate discourse rather than personal attack — but the avoidant conflict style means their first instinct would be to withdraw or suppress rather than actively engage with reframing the meaning, making this a good but not perfectly natural choice.
cases.narrative: You feel the anger flare the moment the contradiction lands — public, visible, your position undermined in front of others. The first thing that happens isn't thought. It's suppression. Your face goes still. Your voice, if you were speaking, would stop. The independent part of you locks the door before anyone sees what's behind it — not out of deference, but out of refusal to give them the satisfaction of a reaction. You hold the anger in place, contained, unexpressed. That's the first few seconds: pure modulation, the conservative instinct to not expose yourself while you're off-balance. But you don't stay there. The suppression bought you a pause, and in the pause something more flexible begins to work. You start turning the contradiction over. Being contradicted publicly isn't the same as being wrong publicly — and even if you were wrong, the correction doesn't diminish you unless you let the frame collapse into humiliation. The person who spoke up may have been clumsy, or right, or both. Your position might need revising, or it might hold — but either way, the anger was about the exposure, not the substance. That recognition shifts the weight. The anger thins from a hot, personal affront into something cooler and more navigable — an event that happened to your argument, not to your self. The suppression fades because there's less to suppress. What remains is a quiet, guarded readiness: you'll respond on your terms, when the meaning has settled, not when the sting is still fresh.

cases.label: reappraiser-shame
cases.reasoning: An analytical, high-autonomy personality with bold risk appetite has both the cognitive discipline to reappraise a public failure as a learning opportunity and the self-assurance to not be overwhelmed by shame — strict rules provide the internal framework for principled reframing, and moderate intensity is squarely in reappraisal's effective range.
cases.narrative: You feel the shame arrive whole — not piece by piece but all at once, the way a blush moves faster than thought. The failure was public, which means it isn't just yours anymore; it lives in the eyes of everyone who watched, and your mind is already writing the story they're telling about you. Incompetent. Exposed. The shame pulls your identity toward the failure, tries to make them the same thing — not someone who failed, but a failure. That's the hinge the reappraisal finds. You catch the collapse mid-fall and hold it apart: the event and the self, separated by a thin, deliberate line of reasoning. The failure happened. It was visible. Those are facts. But the narrative your shame is building — that this single moment defines how you're known, that competence lost once is competence lost permanently — is an interpretation, and it's doing more damage than the failure itself. You start to reconstruct. Everyone in that room has failed publicly at something; the ones you respect most have failed spectacularly and kept working. The failure revealed a gap, not a verdict. It showed you where your preparation ended and the real difficulty began, which is information you didn't have before and now do. The shame doesn't dissolve — it loosens. The hot, total exposure feeling cools into something more bounded: embarrassment, maybe, which is smaller and more survivable. You still feel the weight of having been seen at your worst, but the meaning of being seen has shifted from permanent judgement to passing discomfort. The failure stays on the record. It just no longer speaks for the whole of you.

cases.label: mixed-anger
cases.reasoning: A moderate-across-all-axes personality can technically execute reappraisal at moderate intensity, but betrayal of trust is a deeply relational violation for a cooperative orientation — the emotional sting of broken cooperation resists clean reframing, and this personality's lack of strong analytical or high-autonomy traits means they don't have the cognitive leverage to convincingly reappraise something that strikes at their core cooperative value; response modulation or situation modification (distancing from the betrayer) would feel more natural.
cases.narrative: You feel the anger land like a door slamming — the betrayal sharp, specific, personal. Someone you trusted used that trust against you, and the cooperative part of you recoils not just from the act but from the violation of the contract you thought you shared. Your first move is to hold still. The suppression is brief, instinctive — a beat of silence where you swallow the first thing you'd say, because the cooperative reflex knows that words thrown in anger damage relationships in ways you'll have to repair later. It's not much of a wall, but it holds long enough. And then the reappraisal opens like a second room behind the first. This is where you're strong — this is the machinery that comes most naturally to you. You begin to disassemble the betrayal. Trust is a bet, and bets can lose without the game being rigged. Did they intend harm, or did their interests simply diverge from yours in a way they handled badly? The anger assumed malice; the reappraisal asks whether incompetence or desperation fits the evidence better. You find, almost immediately, that it might. The cooperative lens you see through isn't naive — it's calculative in its own way, running the cost-benefit of maintaining the relationship against the cost of the breach. The betrayal still happened. But its meaning has shifted from an attack on you to a failure of the other person — their inability to navigate the tension between what they needed and what they owed you. The anger drains substantially, replaced by something more like disappointed clarity. You see them more accurately now: not an enemy, but someone whose reliability has a boundary you didn't know about until they crossed it. The relationship isn't over, but its terms have changed, and you feel the new terms settling into place with a steadiness that surprises you.

cases.label: compounding-shame
cases.reasoning: While attentional deployment is normally a natural fit for this avoidant profile, the 4th episode of recurring shame signals that avoidance-based strategies have been failing to resolve the underlying cause — this personality would still gravitate toward distraction, but repeated failure accumulates into a pattern where even an avoidant person's natural strategy becomes less effective, and response modulation (quiet withdrawal to protect self-image) becomes the more instinctive self-protective move for chronic shame.
cases.temporalReasoning: Primarily temporal containment — the narrative depicts the same attentional withdrawal and riding-out strategy, now degraded by repetition, but the closing recognition that 'turning away won't be enough' and deferred self-evaluation is 'accumulating interest' introduces a meta-awareness that edges toward acknowledging future reappraisal will be needed, without actually executing any cognitive restructuring in the present moment.
cases.shameDepthReasoning: The depth perfectly matches an avoidant, low-autonomy suppressor facing compounded shame — the narrative shows withdrawal as the primary strategy but captures its erosion over four episodes without ever breaking into genuine introspection, exactly as this personality would process: aware the strategy is failing yet still unable to pivot to real self-examination, with the deferred self-evaluation framed as accumulating debt rather than something actively engaged.
cases.narrative: You feel the shame arrive and it brings company — not just this failure but the shadows of three before it, each one stirring in the silt as the new one lands. The weight is cumulative now. Your usual withdrawal — the quiet pulling-away, the redirection of attention to something safer — has been your answer each time, and each time it worked a little less. The shame knows the route now. It follows you when you turn away, finds you in the next task, whispers through the thing you tried to focus on instead. You feel the fatigue of a strategy wearing thin, the diminishing returns of a door you've closed four times on something that keeps learning to knock louder. So the withdrawal this time is different — not the smooth redirection but something more ragged, more effortful. You pull your attention sideways but it stutters, catches on the accumulated evidence that you keep ending up here. The corridor you've been escaping into is getting shorter. You manage it — you find something to hold your focus, a handhold outside the spiral — but the grip is weaker, and you can feel the shame sitting patient just outside the beam of your attention, closer than it was the first time, or the second. The regulation holds, but barely. Something in you recognises that the next time this lands, turning away won't be enough. The strategy that protected you is approaching its limit, and the self-evaluation you've been deferring is accumulating interest you'll eventually have to pay.

cases.label: relational-shame
cases.reasoning: This personality has strong reappraisal machinery — analytical, high autonomy, bold — and moderate intensity is well within range, but shame from disappointing a deeply respected mentor creates a values-alignment tension that resists clean reframing: strict rule-following means they genuinely believe they fell short of a legitimate standard, and reappraising the failure's meaning risks feeling like rationalization rather than principled reasoning, making situation modification (concrete corrective action to restore the mentor's trust) a slightly more natural first impulse for this action-oriented profile.
cases.shameDepthReasoning: The depth is precisely calibrated for an analytical reappraiser with high autonomy and bold risk tolerance — the narrative engages in genuine, sophisticated cognitive reappraisal (reframing disappointment as expectation, not contempt) while the relational charging from the high-intimacy mentor relationship creates appropriate resistance to full resolution, leaving the shame partially reframed but not dismissed, exactly matching how an analytical personality would process relationally-weighted shame: deeply, honestly, with structural insight but without emotional bypassing.
cases.narrative: You feel the shame sink deeper than it should — deeper than the failure warrants on its own — because it's their face you see when you look at what you did wrong. Not a colleague, not a stranger, but the person whose opinion you've built part of yourself around, whose standards you internalised so thoroughly that disappointing them feels like disappointing a version of yourself you were trying to become. The shame has a relational weight that makes it heavier than its intensity alone accounts for. It's not just that you fell short — it's that you fell short in front of the person whose gaze you most wanted to be worthy of. The reappraisal starts slowly, working against resistance, because reframing a mentor's disappointment feels dangerously close to dismissing it. But you find the thread. The closeness that makes their judgement devastating is the same closeness that means they've seen you fail before and stayed. A mentor who invests at this depth doesn't invest in a finished product — they invest in the arc, and arcs include these moments. The disappointment you're imagining in their eyes might be real, but disappointment from someone who cares about your growth is categorically different from contempt. It carries expectation, not rejection. You feel the reframe take partial hold — partial, because the intimacy resists full cognitive reworking. You can tell yourself that mentors expect failure, and believe it, and still feel the particular sting of being less than you wanted to be in the presence of someone who showed you what more looked like. The shame doesn't resolve. It softens from a verdict into a tension — the productive, uncomfortable kind that lives inside relationships deep enough to survive what you did.

cases.label: surface-shame
cases.reasoning: High grandiosity and callousness create a personality that instinctively suppresses shame displays and projects composure or deflection when caught — response modulation isn't just natural here, it's practically automatic; this personality lacks the self-reflective vulnerability needed for reappraisal and has no motivation to distract from something they barely internalize in the first place.
cases.shameDepthReasoning: The shallow, deflective processing perfectly matches high grandiosity (0.8) and callousness (0.8) — shame is rejected at the gate rather than internalized, externalized onto others ('they put you in that position'), reframed as inconvenience rather than moral failure, with pre-assembled rationalization and zero genuine self-evaluation, exactly how a grandiose-callous personality would handle shame: a one-second flicker immediately overwritten by contempt and entitlement.
cases.narrative: You feel the shame flicker — a brief, hot flash of exposure, the involuntary recognition that you've been seen doing something beneath you. It lasts about a second. Then the machinery kicks in, smooth and practised, and it's less regulation than reflex: the shame doesn't get suppressed so much as rejected at the gate. Your face rearranges itself — not into contrition but into something harder, something that says this isn't what it looks like, or if it is, it doesn't matter the way they think it does. The lie was necessary. They put you in a position where honesty would have been naive. Anyone in your shoes would have done the same — they just wouldn't have been caught. The exposure stings, but what stings is the being caught, not the lying. The self-evaluation that shame requires — the turning inward, the measuring of yourself against a standard and finding yourself short — simply doesn't engage. The standard doesn't apply to you, or the standard is wrong, or the situation was exceptional. The rationalisation isn't effortful; it arrives pre-assembled, a script you've run so many times it plays automatically. What reaches the surface is mild irritation at the inconvenience of being caught, maybe a flicker of contempt for whoever noticed. The shame itself is already gone — not processed, not worked through, just turned away at the door like something that showed up at the wrong address. You move on. There's nothing underneath to sit with, because you didn't let it get underneath.
